pages.text: After the war in Nagorno-Karabakh ended, a ceasefire agreement was signed on ten November 2020. Russia sent a peacekeeping group to the region to watch the ceasefire between Armenian and Azerbaijani forces. This group had nearly two thousand soldiers led by Lieutenant General Rustam Muradov. They set up posts along the contact line and near Stepanakert.

The Russian peacekeepers started helping the Red Cross to find and exchange fallen soldiers. Later, they also began demining the region to make it safer. Turkey and Russia agreed to create a joint monitoring center. Turkey sent sappers and officers to help with demining and training. The monitoring center opened at the end of January 2021.

However, the region faced many challenges and ceasefire violations. Clashes happened near some villages in the Hadrut Province. These villages became a holdout during the fighting. The Russian peacekeeping contingent briefly took control of one village before it came under Azerbaijani control. Both sides accused each other of restarting the conflict.

Over time, more incidents caused worry and international criticism. In late 2021, a civilian was killed during farm work by shelling. In 2022, armed forces entered the territory and set up an observation post, leading to drone strikes and casualties. Russia publicly assigned blame to Azerbaijan for violating the agreement. Later, Azerbaijani forces withdrew from one village.

In March 2023, during an ongoing blockade, Azerbaijani forces crossed the line of contact again. They occupied a strategic height and brought engineering equipment. The Russian peacekeepers asked them to stop and withdraw. Meanwhile, Azerbaijan stated their forces took control measures to stop the transport of military means on dirt roads.

Following the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, a trilateral ceasefire agreement was signed on 10 November 2020. In accordance with this accord, Russia deployed a peacekeeping contingent consisting of nearly two thousand servicemen to the region. Led by Lieutenant General Rustam Muradov and headquartered near Stepanakert, these forces established observation posts along the contact line and the Lachin corridor to monitor the ceasefire between Armenian and Azerbaijani forces.

Alongside the Russian mission, Turkey and Russia established a joint monitoring center near Marzili in Azerbaijan. Turkish sappers and officers arrived to assist with demining operations and train local personnel. The monitoring center officially opened on 30 January 2021, utilizing unmanned aerial vehicles and personnel from both nations to monitor ceasefire compliance under the guard of Azerbaijani soldiers.

Despite the presence of peacekeepers, significant violations occurred. Clashes erupted near Hadrut around an Artsakh holdout pocket comprising specific villages and a monastery. After initial confusion and brief Russian control, the villages ultimately came under Azerbaijani control, with both sides trading blame for the renewed violence.

Tensions persisted through subsequent years. In October 2021, a local civilian was killed by cross-border shelling during agricultural work, prompting investigations and mutual accusations. In March 2022, Azerbaijani forces entered the territory, resulting in drone strikes and casualties. For the first time, the Russian Ministry of Defence publicly blamed Azerbaijan for violating the ceasefire agreement, though disputes over subsequent troop withdrawals remained.

By March 2023, amidst a prolonged blockade, peacekeepers reported that Azerbaijani forces had crossed the line of contact, occupied a strategic height, and set up engineering equipment. Russia requested a withdrawal to previous positions, while Azerbaijan maintained that its actions were necessary to suppress military transportation along northern dirt roads.

In the wake of the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, a ceasefire agreement precipitated the deployment of a Russian peacekeeping contingent comprising 1,960 servicemen under the command of Lieutenant General Rustam Muradov. Headquartered near Stepanakert, the contingent established observation posts along the contact line and the Lachin corridor. Concurrently, a separate Russian-Turkish Joint Monitoring Centre was initiated to provide remote monitoring capabilities through unmanned aerial vehicles and bilateral personnel stationed in Azerbaijan.

Initial humanitarian mandates included assisting the International Committee of the Red Cross with the exchange of fallen soldiers and initiating comprehensive demining operations. However, the mission immediately encountered geopolitical friction. Azerbaijani authorities criticized the peacekeepers for exhibiting a perceived pro-Armenian bias, pointing to leadership engagements with local officials and the contested use of administrative terminology, which strained the intended neutrality of the deployment.

The fragility of the cessation of hostilities was underscored by localized military engagements. Armed clashes materialized around an Artsakh holdout pocket in the Hadrut Province. Despite initial Russian intervention, disputed territorial demarcations resulted in specific villages falling under Azerbaijani control amid reciprocal accusations of ceasefire violations.

Subsequent years witnessed recurrent kinetic incidents and escalating humanitarian crises. In October 2021, fatal shelling during agricultural work triggered diplomatic recriminations regarding targeted displacement. A more acute escalation occurred in March 2022 when Azerbaijani units crossed the line of contact, precipitating drone strikes and casualties. Notably, this prompted Russia to publicly attribute ceasefire violations directly to Azerbaijan, diverging from prior diplomatic ambiguities.

By March 2023, during an ongoing blockade that drew international censure, peacekeepers documented further territorial advancements by Azerbaijani forces across the line of contact. While Russian command formally requested a withdrawal of national armed forces to prior positions, Azerbaijan defended its deployment as a localized measure to interdict military supply routes, highlighting the persistent limitations of the peacekeeping architecture.
